props.title: The Comedy of Terrors
props.initialSlug: Undertaker plots murders to drum up business

sections.content: The Comedy of Terrors (1963) represents a delicious dark comedy reunion of horror titans Vincent Price, Peter Lorre, and Boris Karloff, following their success in Tales of Terror (1962). Director Jacques Tourneur, fresh from psychological horror masterpiece Night of the Demon (1957), brings his atmospheric touch to this macabre tale of an unscrupulous undertaker who drums up business by murdering potential clients. The film perfectly balances horror-comedy elements while showcasing Price at his hammiest best, delivering Shakespeare quotes with gleeful menace.

sections.content: The early 1960s saw American International Pictures (AIP) deliberately mixing horror with dark humor, moving away from their straight Gothic Poe adaptations like House of Usher (1960). The Comedy of Terrors represents this shift perfectly, maintaining the period setting and macabre atmosphere while letting its veteran cast play their roles with knowing wit. The film particularly benefits from the genuine chemistry between Price and Lorre, whose partnership had been honed through multiple AIP productions.

What elevates The Comedy of Terrors beyond mere camp is Richard Matheson's clever screenplay. The writer behind I Am Legend (1954) and numerous Twilight Zone episodes crafts sharp dialogue that allows the cast to shine while maintaining legitimate horror elements. Joyce Jameson's operatic interludes and Basil Rathbone's Shakespeare-quoting insomnia victim add layers of theatrical absurdity that complement the funeral parlor setting. SUBHEAD: The Legacy of Horror-Comedy

sections.content: The Comedy of Terrors helped establish a template for horror-comedies that would influence films for decades to come. Its influence can be seen in later works like Young Frankenstein (1974) and Murder by Death (1976), where classic horror elements are treated with both reverence and irreverence. The film's approach to death as both terrifying and absurd would later echo in works like Arsenic and Old Lace (1944) and modern horror-comedies like What We Do in the Shadows (2014).
